title: Fifty Must-Know Crucial Golden Nuggets About AI And The Law That You Need To Know
text:
In today’s column, I will be providing a sweeping grand tour of the burgeoning field encompassing AI and the law. I aim to provide a forest for the trees type of elicitation. This hopefully will be particularly useful to lawyers and law firms, along with potentially being informative too for lawmakers, regulators, and all manner of non-lawyers that are interested in the latest facets entailing AI and the law.
I’ve opted to showcase fifty of the must-know crucial topics about AI and the law. My basis for selecting these fifty is based on what readers tend to ask me about and also as customarily comes up when I speak at conferences and industry events on AI and the law. Notably, I could have made this a much longer list and easily gone into the hundred or higher range of worthy topics. Space limitations herein necessitate I must agonizingly choose the biggest bang for the buck in terms of topics to cover.
Approach To This Analysis
Speaking of space limitations, for each topic I aimed to succinctly say what the topic is about and why it is important. I have covered all of these topics in my various columns and papers, so I’ve indicated links to those materials in case you want to dig deeper into a given topic. If all goes well, you will feel informed and somewhat inspired to learn more about this exciting domain.
Another nuance to keep in mind is that we are experiencing a rapid evolution of AI and law that is rather unprecedented. My expertise in this field goes back well over twenty years and during that time the field has slowly inched its way forward. The recent advent of generative AI as a widely and wildly popular tool has sparked an unrelenting horserace toward advancing AI and ergo equally prodded the field of AI and law into supersonic speeds. Much of what I mention in this discussion is subject to ongoing change and advancement.
As with any field of endeavor, there are often strong opinions that go along with each of the AI and the law topics discussed. Those opinions can be diametrically opposed to each other. I have carefully attempted to provide a balanced viewpoint (most of the time) so that you can ultimately do your own added research and decide for yourself which side of the proverbial coin you wish to land on. Admittedly, my own viewpoint slips into the picture here and there. Please bear with me on that occasional blend.
A couple of other heads-ups might be handy for you.
Some say that AI is a fad and that we will soon tire of the AI mania underway. I completely disagree with this sentiment. The reality is that we are on a conveyer belt that is going to keep pushing us along on advancing AI and leveraging AI into all quarters of society. No one is going to be able to turn back the clock. The genie is clearly out of the bottle. All of this has deep ramifications for AI and the law. Though it might sound like a trope, there is assuredly avid and pointed transformation and disruption coming along on the emergent AI and law front.
The sequence of my below set of topics is intended to roughly tie together the myriad of subtopics and tell an overall story about the breadth and depth of AI and the law. That being said, you can pretty much jump around throughout the list and still garner the essence of each subtopic (I’ve sought to make each elucidation semi-independent of the other subtopics). Read those that catch your eye. You might not have the time or inclination to get through the whole exposition. Though, I must say, if you can digest and mindfully contemplate the entire set, I proffer a hearty congratulations. You ought to proudly pat yourself on the back for having begun a foremost journey. You will have gotten a breathtaking and wide-sweeping overview of AI and law under your belt.
A considered next step for you would be to follow up and explore further any particular subtopics that suit your fancy. Also, I’m ready if readers of today’s column want me to do a follow-up and cover even more topics on AI and the law, I’ll earnestly do so. Be on the watch for that.
AI And The Law: Crucial Topics
The first three topics that I am going cover, numbered as items one to three below, are my stated “big picture” of AI and law. I’d highly recommend you start with those three. It should provide an insightful macroscopic perspective that will aid you throughout the later perusal of the densely wooded forest. Items numbered 4 through 26 focus on the matter of the law being applied to AI, while the remainder of items numbered 27 through 45 focus on the application of AI to the law.
I will proceed directly into each topic and then at the very end provide a list of the entire set. Why not show the whole list upfront? Here’s the deal. I don’t want you to unduly be fretting at the get-go that the list seems dauntingly long, plus at the end, you’ll feel quite accomplished and be able to do a mental check mark of the remarkable adventurous journey you undertook.
Good luck and enjoy the voyage.
(1) Defining AI and the law
There is some confusion about what it means to refer to AI and the law. Allow me to clear that up. I describe AI and the law as consisting of two categories that intertwine or dovetail together the respective fields of AI and the law, namely that you can apply the law to AI, and likewise, you can seek to apply AI to the law.
Here’s what I mean:
- The law applied to AI: Consists of applying the law to AI for purposes of governing, guiding, and otherwise leveraging the law to try and ensure that AI is devised and utilized according to legal means.
- AI applied to the law: Consists of applying AI to the law such as aiding lawyers via AI-based apps or potentially having AI perform legal tasks directly.
As indicated, you can handily divide this world up into those two buckets. You would also likely discover that by and large most people versed in AI and the law tend to concentrate on one of those buckets more so than the other. Some care deeply about the law as applied to AI, and they are less interested in AI as applied to the law. Others are steeped in AI applied to the law and less interested in the law as applied to AI.
You can choose your own cup of tea.
As a general rule of thumb, though exceptions are aplenty, lawyers that are not especially into AI technology seem to gravitate toward the law as applied to AI camp, assuming they get interested in AI at all. For them, the intriguing challenge involves how laws will or ought to impact the design, building, testing, and fielding of AI. Meanwhile, lawyers that have some kind of tech-oriented background will often seem to lean toward the application of AI in the legal field. They are fascinated by and curious about how far AI can go toward performing legal tasks. They want to know whether AI is coming for their job and whether AI is going to change how legal work is undertaken.
Of course, this bifurcation is not written in stone and many relish delving into both camps.
For more on the fundamentals of AI and the law, see my coverage at the link here.
(2) Synergy of AI and the law
Let’s revisit the two camps underlying AI and the law.
You’ve got lawyers and law firms that have opted to put attention toward facets of how the law can be applied to AI, including interpreting existing laws, regulations, and new laws that aim to rein in abuses undertaken via AI systems. They might be serving clients that are AI makers, or non-tech clients that simply are adopting AI in their firms (and potentially faced with legal issues associated with their use of AI, now or in the near future).
The other camp is lawyers and law firms that are keenly interested in applying AI to legal tasks. They might seek to use AI to write contracts or analyze legal cases or do e-discovery. They might aim to purchase LegalTech software that has AI built-in or bolted-on. Some of these efforts are pilots and prototypes, others are all out adoptions of AI capabilities.
Much of the time, those two camps are each of their own devotion.
That being said, there is definitely a synergy associated with duality. Lawyers and law firms that start in one camp are bound to ease their way into the other camp. For example, some would vehemently argue that lawyers and law firms that focus on the law as applied to AI would be wise to also apply AI to the law, such that they would get a first-hand grasp of what it is like to adopt and utilize AI. Thus, the hands-on activity would enrich their ability to comprehend how to interpret laws associated with AI. The other direction holds water too. The act of adopting AI by a law firm or lawyers is almost assuredly going to get their mental juices going about the legal ins and outs associated with using AI technology.
There’s an added synergistic impact, perhaps riskily or beneficially, depending on how managed.
Law firms and lawyers that adopt AI are going to look quite foolish if they aren’t also up-to-speed about the laws associated with AI. Consider this. Suppose a law firm adopts AI for use in the hiring of personnel at the law firm. Imagine if the AI contained discriminatory practices. Along comes a federal agency overseeing such maladies that blast the law firm, which, takes an especially tough bruising in the legal and business world. The reputational damage could have the tail wagging the dog, namely a lack of attention to the legal dynamics of AI that caught them on their own petard.
A counterviewpoint to all of this by some law firms and lawyers is that maybe it is best to stay out of the fray entirely. Don’t join either camp. Don’t get involved in AI at all. Wait and see how things pan out for others. Only once the grass is green will you hop on board. That head-in-the-sand strategy might be workable for some, but the trouble is that the rest of the legal world might pass you by before you know it. Other law firms and lawyers that have gotten into AI, one camp or another, will be better positioned and be first movers that leave the crumbs for those that are later on AI and law tagalongs.
A popular refrain these days is that it isn’t the possibility that AI might replace lawyers outright is where your mental contemplations should go, but instead, the eye on the ball is that lawyers and law firms equipped with and savvy about AI that is going to eclipse lawyers and law firms that aren’t savvy about AI
I find this reminiscent of the old witticism about two campers in the woods that inadvertently meander upon and startle a now angry bear. One camper immediately starts running away. The other camper yells out that it is not feasible to outrun a bear. The camper running at full speed yells back over their shoulder and tells their fellow camper that outrunning the bear isn’t the goal, and instead, the goal is to outrun their fellow camper. Lawyers and law firms adopting AI are potentially going to outrun those lawyers and law firms that aren’t adopting AI.
(3) Clarifying what AI consists of (it’s not just generative AI)
AI means different things to different people. Those that have come upon AI via the use of generative AI such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, Bard, Claude, or the like, often perceive that AI is always and only generative AI.
They would be mistaken.
This is akin to coming upon an elephant and after touching the trunk, you declare that any animal with a trunk is irrefutably an elephant (tapirs, saiga antelopes, giant anteaters, proboscis monkeys, and other animals would be dismayed or at least confused if you told them face-to-face they are elephants).
AI can be said to be aspirational verbiage that expresses a desire to devise computers that can exhibit human-like intelligence. Because the catchphrase of AI kept getting battered around in recent times, the AI field came up with a new piece of terminology to express the aspirational AI, known nowadays as Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Thus, in a sense, you are supposed to say AGI when talking about the futuristic sentient AI. The rest of the time the reference to AI is basically today’s conventional non-sentient AI.
Another way to conceive of AI is as a constellation of advanced technologies that individually and collectively are hoped to someday get us to AGI.
The umbrella of technologies that tend to be classified as within the domain of AI include but are not limited to:
- Generative AI
- Large Language Models
- Machine Learning
- Deep Learning
- Knowledge-based Systems
- Expert Systems
- Robotics
- Natural Language Processing
- Common-Sense Reasoning
- Speech Recognition
- Machine Vision Processing
- Autonomous Systems
- Other
I want to emphasize that those technologies are not purely distinctive per se and they readily overlap with each other. Some believe that the only viable path to AGI entails leveraging them all together in some as yet unknown fashion. Others insist that we have not yet discovered the secret sauce technology that is required for AGI. They assert that this unknown ingredient will potentially work alongside the above set of tech or will be self-sufficient and not require any of the rest of today’s AI technologies.
Why should you care about any of this confounding morass about what we mean when referring to AI?
Because crafting laws and regulations pertaining to AI must presumably be able to definitively articulate what they are seeking to cover. If you can’t pin it down, any laws supposedly pertinent to the matter will be legally readily attacked by the simple posture that those laws don’t apply to the alleged AI in hand. A retort is that you ought to then make laws that cast a wide net and will encompass anything even remotely smelling of AI. Definitions of AI are a dime a dozen. When a new AI law is being crafted, one never knows how that particular legal author will opt to define AI. It makes a huge difference. If a given law posits a definition of AI that is askew, it can cover everything under the sun and overstate what AI is. If the definition is overly narrow, whatever was hoped to be curtailed about AI will likely slip through.
Many of the AI laws being put together give scant attention to defining AI within the scope of the crafted law. They toss something into the bill and give no mind to it. This lack of attention to a foundational matter will rear its head later on, once the bill goes into effect. Up until then, the definition will seem inconsequential.
The irony is that the definition of AI in the new law, or possibly a lack of a definition, will indubitably become a pivotal legal issue for those that argue either in favor of or in opposition to the meaning of the law during court cases. No one will especially remember that the included definition of AI was a tiny and seemingly insignificant element when the law was being crafted.
Get yourself ready for the era of the AI definitional legal debates.
I direct your attention to a federal definition that seems to have generally become popular as a default pattern for defining AI in legal contracts. It was first codified in Section 238(g) of the John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019. Since then, many lawmakers and regulators have gone the easy road by merely copying and pasting the AI definition into their contracts.
Here’s the definition:
- “(g) ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE DEFINED. In this section, the term ‘‘artificial intelligence’’ includes the following: 1) Any artificial system that performs tasks under varying and unpredictable circumstances without significant human oversight, or that can learn from experience and improve performance when exposed to data sets; 2) An artificial system developed in computer software, physical hardware, or other context that solves tasks requiring human-like perception, cognition, planning, learning, communication, or physical action; 3) An artificial system designed to think or act like a human, including cognitive architectures and neural networks; 4) A set of techniques, including machine learning, that is designed to approximate a cognitive task; 5) An artificial system designed to act rationally, including an intelligent software agent or embodied robot that achieves goals using perception, planning, reasoning, learning, communicating, decision-making, and acting.”
Can you spot the various loopholes?

Those on the hook will be legal entities and actual humans throughout the entire AI supply chain or AI value chain, such as the AI makers, AI implementers, AI deployers, and the like.
(26) Legal wranglings over AI will be a giant boon to AI-savvy lawyers and law firms
For the preceding reasons articulated in my numbered items of one through 25, I believe a strong and logical case can be made that legal wrangling over AI will be a giant boon to AI-savvy lawyers and law firms. Unless the clock gets turned back and we all decide to demote and reduce the making and spreading of AI, AI is here to stay and will decidedly be ubiquitous in our daily lives.
(27) AI as applied to the law is growing immensely
We will switch hats now and consider the application of AI to the law.
This is another rapidly growing area and you should anticipate that it too isn’t going to somehow slow down or evaporate. Do not close your eyes and hope that maybe AI will just disappear from being used in the law. No chance.
AI is right now being devised and put into use to aid lawyers and law firms. This will continue. AI will be further advanced to do even better at aiding legal tasks. This will increase AI adoption in the legal field. We will also see the encroachment of a sort, consisting of AI that performs legal tasks without any need for human intervention or assistance.
I’m going to be a bit more succinct for the remainder of these depictions. Again, I’ll provide links so that you can dive deeper.
(28) Infusing AI into legal practices and all manner of tasks at hand
Using AI in the law is often instinctively viewed in a rather narrow sense, perhaps the use of AI for devising contracts or maybe aiding e-discovery.
The more appropriate perspective is to consider the use of AI across all legal tasks, such as the list shown here:
- Case Management
- Contracts
- Courts & Trials
- Discovery
- Documents/Records
- Intellectual Property (IP)
- Law Office/Practice
- Lawyer & Client Interaction
- Legal Assistants
- Legal Collaboration
- Legal Research
- Legal Workflow
- Legal Writing
- Professional Conduct
- Other
Basically, any legal task done by a legal professional or performed in a law firm is entirely subject to the inclusion of AI. This doesn’t necessarily mean that you replace a human worker with AI. Depending upon the legal expertise associated with the legal task, the AI might serve as a partial aid, a more bolstered aid, or possibly even tackle a great deal of the legal tasks, though subject to the oversight and review of a human attorney (for now).
See more of my coverage at the link here.
(29) LegalTech getting paired with AI will be the new norm
The legal market has its own specialized systems.
Software and computer-based systems oriented toward lawyers can potentially encompass the full range of legal tasks performed by law firms. Systems in this domain are commonly referred to as LegalTech (similarly named as MedTech, FinTech, and other such categories for other professional domains).
By and large, much of today’s LegalTech is focused on one-and-done legal tasks, such as aiding the contract life cycle or doing only e-discovery, performing just one specific legal task. Fewer do you see across-the-board enterprise systems that cover the entire gamut of all legal tasks (I’m not saying this doesn’t exist, and nor am I suggesting that it isn’t being pursued avidly).
Many lawyers and law firms have been slow to adopt and utilize LegalTech. Trying to then get AI into the picture can be arduous since the lack of already in-use LegalTech boasts added challenges when trying to include AI capabilities. Vendors of LegalTech products are hurriedly adding AI to their wares. The idea is that rather than a law firm or lawyer having to figure out how to establish AI on their own, they will already have it included in their purchased or licensed LegalTech.
I characterize the LegalTech offerings into three eras:
- Era #1: Conventional LegalTech (has no AI at all)
- Era #2: AI-Augmented LegalTech (AI added into LegalTech)
- Era #3: Infused AI With LegalTech (AI at the core of LegalTech)
You can anticipate that the use of AI in LegalTech will become the norm.
See more of my coverage at the link here.
(30) Lawyers that aren’t in the know can blindside themselves and their law firm
A recent and widely publicized tale of woe occurred when two lawyers made use of generative AI and got themselves into legal hot water, doing so by their own lack of awareness about AI. They had used ChatGPT to generate an indication of prior legal cases pertinent to a legal matter they were arguing in an active court case. The generative AI generated fictitious legal cases (this is a type of AI issue coined as an AI hallucination). The lawyers submitted the legal cases as though the cases were real. Sparks flew, as you might imagine.
Lessons you should learn from the tale of woe is that law firms would be wise to do this:
- Explore how AI can be used by lawyers and legal professionals at their law firm
- Establish a sensible set of internal policies and procedures in your law firm about AI usage
- Set up an internal committee to aid in the ongoing upkeep of the AI policies and procedures
- Mindfully communicate to your lawyers and other professionals about the AI policies and procedures
- Undertake suitable training for any AI-related use that is undertaken in the law firm
- Sensibly track AI usage and adjust accordingly your AI policies and procedures
- And so on
For my coverage of the tale of woe, see the link here.
For my coverage of the reaction by some judges to stipulating new rules for lawyers in their court, see the link here.
(31) Judges are just beginning to pushback on AI use by lawyers
Per the tale of woe about two lawyers and their use of AI (mentioned above), a handful of judges subsequently opted on their own to establish policies in their respective courts about the use of AI by attorneys coming before their court. You can anticipate more of this happening.
Be prepared. Make sure that you know what if any provisions the court has established about AI usage for the courts you are practicing law in. Abide by it, or face the wrath and penalties that might arise. Also, as a handy tip, you don’t want the reputational damage that will be a fallout of getting caught failing to dutifully use AI in the proper ways.
(32) Law firms stepping up to establish policies and procedures on the internal use of AI
Law firms can readily establish policies and procedures about the internal use of AI. It is easy to do. And should be done, right away. The longer you wait, the greater the exposure.
Now then, merely writing up such a document is not the end of the story. You need to make sure that it is sensible, workable, understandable, and practical. You need to communicate what it is. You need to aid your attorneys in abiding by it. You need to track and see whether it is being observed. You need to adjust it as the AI technology changes.
Do not falsely believe that you can just write something down and wash your hands of the matter. Bad practice.
(33) Use of generative AI can impact the revered attorney-client privilege
If a lawyer uses a generative AI app to aid in brainstorming about a case in hand, and if the generative AI retains the entered data about the case, and the data is perchance subsequently seen by others such as the AI maker, does that potentially usurp the revered attorney-client privilege?
Suppose the client uses generative AI and describes their legal case to the AI, does that potentially usurp the revered attorney-client privilege?
My coverage of this engaging topic is found at the link here.
(34) AI will inevitably be applied across all legal domains
Some lawyers assume that AI only applies to particular legal domains, such only for criminal law or corporate law. I assure you that AI is heading toward being used in all of the legal domains, slowly but surely.
Here’s a representative (but not exhaustive) list of legal domains that one way or another are targeted for AI usage:
- Admiralty law
- Animal law
- Antitrust law
- Banking law
- Bankruptcy law
- Civil Rights law
- Constitutional law
- Corporate law
- Criminal law
- Education law
- Employment law
- Entertainment law
- Environmental law
- Family law
- Health law
- Immigration law
- International law
- IP law
- Military law
- Personal injury law
- Real Estate law
- Tax law
- Etc.
See my further coverage at the link here.
(35) Generative AI usage in five sensible initial ways (cautiously)
I consult with law firms and lawyers and advise them to sensibly and cautiously tryout generative AI, such as using AI for these five easy-starter legal-oriented tasks:
- (1) Legal Brainstorming
- (2) Drafting Legal Briefs
- (3) Reviewing Legal Documents
- (4) Summarizing Legal Narratives
- (5) Converting Legalese Into Plain Language
If you are going to do so, please make sure you have done all suitable preparation and precautionary actions, see my discussion at the link here.
(36) Prompt engineering for lawyers using generative AI
When using generative AI, you enter a prompt that the AI responds to by generating or producing an essay or engaging in an interactive dialogue with you. Make sure to sensibly compose your prompts.
Lousy prompts will tend to get lousy results and waste your time and effort. Good prompts will tend to get valued responses. The importance of appropriate prompting has led to the emergence of prompt engineering, providing key guidance about composing prompts.
I’ve been doing a series on prompt engineering, at the link here.
(37) Productizing legal services via codifying lawyering with AI
Lawyers are engaged in a labor-based service.
What if you could bottle that capability and sell it essentially as a product? Your law firm could shift from exclusively a labor-based service delivery business model to a blend of labor and automation doing so, encapsulating both a service capacity and a product capacity. This is typically referred to as productizing legal services (PLS).
Start-ups in the LegalTech space see this same opportunity. So-called lawyering in a can, as it were. I’ve been advising and mentoring starts-up in the legal realm that are strenuously applying AI to the law. Let’s get those unicorns on their way to stardom.
For more on this exciting and emerging trend, see the link here.
(38) Full-on autonomous legal reasoning by AI is harder than it seems
The holy grail of AI being applied to the law consists of devising AI that can fully perform AI-based autonomous legal reasoning, ergo requiring no human assistance or intervention whatsoever. This has been a longstanding research goal and stumped the AI world since the beginning of working on AI.
You might be tempted to think that due to the wonders of generative AI, we must be on the verge of attaining that autonomous legal reasoning. Sorry to report that we are still searching for the means to achieve this altogether very hard and extraordinarily grand challenge.
That being said, you have to be mindful of what it means to say that autonomous legal reasoning is or isn’t here as yet. If a legal problem can be selectively chosen and kept exceedingly narrow, you can somewhat claim that AI for that particular scope could perform the legal task autonomously. The question becomes how small a task is and how narrow it has to be.
Autonomous AI legal reasoning (AILR) is one of my most devoted areas of research and practice, see for example my work at the link here and the link here, just to name a few. For anyone wanting to stretch the limits of today’s AI, doing so in the legal realm is enthralling and tremendously inspiring.
(39) Unauthorized Practice of Law (UPL) moves to center stage due to AI
Suppose we craft AI that can perform some type of legal task. Maybe a small task, such as helping people legally contest a parking ticket. This AI is put into public use and becomes available for a modest fee.
Has this AI legally gone out-of-bounds and violated the authorized practice of law (APL), or as more commonly phrased is this an instance of the unauthorized practice of law (UPL)?
In the United States, we have APL/UPL provisions that are intended to ensure that when you seek and make use of legal services, you are advised by a properly licensed human attorney. This is supposed to be for the good of the public at large. Some question whether this is still prudent. If AI can do a legal task sufficiently, let’s say on par with a human attorney, do we label the AI as violating APL/UPL and get the AI tossed into the junk heap even though it seems to be able to do the legal job?
Tough questions about APL/UPL are afoot, see my analysis at the link here.
(40) Multijurisdictional lawyering in an era of AI applied to the law
In the United States, lawyering is essentially geographically based. Lawyers are customarily supposed to practice in a particular state and usually only do so in that chosen state, though they can at times undertake in selected and strict ways a limited form of multijurisdictional lawyering.
If we devise AI that suitably performs legal tasks in multiple states, having the domain-specific capability in each of those states, could we break out of the state-at-a-time conventional approach and allow for multijurisdictional legal coverage?
For more on this open question, see the link here.
(41) Long predicted trifecta of the robo-lawyer, robo-judge, robo-juror
One of the most talked about and perhaps misused memes about AI applied to the law consists of the proverbial robo-lawyer, an overwrought outdated piece of verbiage. The idea behind this phrasing is that we are going to someday have robots that will be able to do what lawyers do. Of course, we don’t necessarily need to have a walking and gesturing robot, perhaps AI software is sufficient (though, don’t count out the day that we have both, consisting of the AI controlling a robot acting out the role of a lawyer).
A lesser-known and infrequently used moniker is that of a robo-judge. That would be AI that acts in the capacity of a judge. You could argue that we in a sense do this already, such as using AI to ascertain whether a parking ticket should be tossed out or kept in force (being done in some limited ways and particular locales). Once again, we are back to my earlier point about the potential use of autonomous legal reasoning in limited or narrowly scoped realms.
Even less utilized is the verbiage of a robo-juror, which would be an AI-based non-human juror.
A trifecta would be when we arrive at all three, namely robo-lawyers, robo-judges, and robo-jurors. This comes with a lot of controversy, including for each one. Would an AI-based judge lack the emotional sentiment and empathy that human judges have? Some argue that this would be desirable since the judging would be accomplished without the undue influence of emotions and be based solely on the facts of the case. Others scoff at this claim and have various counterarguments. In terms of the robo-jurors, could an AI-only non-human juror suitably serve in a juror capacity, going against our highly prized principle of being judged by a jury of your (human) peers?
For more on the trifecta, see my analysis at the link here.
(42) Data about the law is not particularly ready for prime time
A surprising revelation to those that are new to the study and practice of law is that the data about our laws, including the many laws on the books, legal cases, legal decisions, and the like are generally not readily available on a comprehensive streamlined online basis. Instead, it turns out that some of the data is paper-based and not yet digitized. Some of the data is digitally encoded but not online and stored offline. Some of the data is digital and online but exists in unusual or difficult computerized formats. Some of the data is costly to access. And so on.
This is problematic for AI.
If you want to extensively data-train AI about the law, you need copious amounts of legal data to do so. It is exasperatingly difficult and usually costly to try and collect that data. As such, one of the most daunting roadblocks underpinning the application of AI to the law entails getting the data that would be needed to do the required data training of the AI.
In one sense, you could argue that this data problem is solvable. There isn’t anything new that we need to invent (well unless some clever invention would make this readily feasible to do). The issue is that we would need to find the data, digitize the data, get it into suitable formats, and then have it ready for scanning when doing AI data training. That’s a mouthful. The logistics are enormous. The cost would be sky-high.
Some question whether we ought to just give up on the data collection path and find a different way to get the AI up-to-speed.
For my analysis of this thorny topic, see the link here.
(43) Law firms waking up to their own trove of data
If you want to use AI for doing legal tasks, one presumed precondition is that the AI needs to be data-trained in the law. One perspective is to generally train AI on the law overall, such as say using all of the US Supreme Court cases or similar overarching bodies or troves of databases about the law.
Another consideration comes to the fore regarding the law as it is embodied by a particular law firm. A law firm that wants to use AI for aiding their legal tasks might be willing to use a generalized AI that covers broadly some areas of law. The odds are though that you would want the AI to also be steeped in the legal aspects as found within your law firm.
Naturally, a law firm would want to be cautious about feeding its own legal-oriented data into an AI system. Would the data be secure? Would the data be misused? Etc. In addition, the potential logistics nightmare and cost to do so is an issue. On the other hand, if a law firm is already principally digitally up-to-speed, the leveraging of their data might not be especially onerous.
For my analysis on this, see the link here.
(44) Is advancing AI a crisis or an opportunity for lawyers
Are advances in AI amid the application of AI to the law a wonderous opportunity for lawyers and law firms, or is it a crisis and possibly a death knell for the legal profession as we know it today?
I get asked this question quite a bit by law students, sensibly so.
They want to know what their future prospects are. Enduring the years of training to be a lawyer and suffering through passing the bar exam, along with cutting your teeth as a junior lawyer, it’s a long and exhausting haul. A person of rational thinking would only do this if the payoff down the road was worthwhile.
My answer is that a career in the legal profession is still a green light. What I also add, in the same breath, is that ignoring or downplaying the upcoming transformation and disruption due to AI is a failing that will likely gum up your legal career pursuits. Make sure to get AI under your belt. Furthermore, enlightened law firms consider this a big plus, assuming that you sensibly know about AI and don’t go overboard about AI.
For my further discussion about this topic, see the link here.
(45) Peering into the minds of judges via the use of AI Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP)
AI can be used to analyze the patterns of judges regarding their judicial decisions and demeanors. This is going to be further heightened as the data about judges gets increasingly digitized and available for data training of AI. All in all, this type of AI-based analysis is usually coined as legal judgment prediction (LJP).
Is it appropriate to put judges under an AI microscope or is this intrusive?
Will judges opt to change their behavior if they know that they are being AI scrutinized?
Some say that all is fair in love and war, including judicial efforts to win your legal cases. Others clamor that the courts should put their foot down and not allow this, though doing so would certainly be contested in our courts as an overreach by the courts.
For some details about this, see my coverage at the link here.
(46) Law firm rankings might get stirred due to AI-empowered lawyering
I’ve predicted that once AI becomes more pervasive in being applied to the law, the chances are that law firms and lawyers will be increasingly assessed on their proficiency in using AI to aid in their legal endeavors.
This makes sense.
If AI can speed up legal tasks, make legal tasks more thorough, provide more extensive legal contemplation and brainstorming, and the like, clients will naturally tend to gravitate toward lawyers and law firms that have productively adopted AI. Firms that haven’t done so or that have made a mess of adopting AI will seemingly be dinged in comparison.
Lawyers and law firms often wait with bated breath for the various rankings of lawyers and law firms. In my view, the use of AI will end up being included as a factor in those rankings. Not today, but once we get closer to the wider use of AI in the law.
See my discussion at the link here.
(47) Law firms and lawyers can wait or act now, their choice in the matter
Can law firms and lawyers wait to decide whether to make use of AI in the law?
In a sense, yes, there is nothing that compels lawyers or law firms to at all dip a toe into AI (as a side note, the ABA has provisions that urge lawyers and law firms to get up-to-speed about AI, which though not necessarily in a compulsory way, does suggest the importance of knowing about AI). They can merrily sit on the sidelines. Their bet or hope is that they can leap into the fray once the use of AI in the law has suitably proven itself.
A potential downside to this waiting strategy is that they might miss the boat and lose out to other lawyers and law firms that have progressed into AI and the law. It’s a competitive thing. Assuming that a learning curve is required, which is indeed the case, the law firm will find itself having to first undertake the initial throes. It won’t be plug-and-play. They will be behind the eight ball.
In addition, the odds are that some or many of the lawyers in a law firm are bound to explore AI on their own, assuming that the law firm has opted to take no action. I think you can see what happens in that instance, such as the two lawyers that made use of ChatGPT and got themselves and their law firm into a bind. Leaving a vacuum means that untoward things can occur, which, notably, you could have easily prevented at the get-go.
Another consideration is whether using AI might be an attractor for legal talent.
Consider this. How can a law firm get the best of the best? Money is one answer, though this usually is roughly about the same across competitors and does not provide a ready standout for luring equally qualified candidates. One factor potentially is that a law firm is adopting AI and providing training and opportunity for their lawyers to leverage AI. This then sparks candidates that have heard about AI or wondered about AI, along with those that already are avidly immersed in AI for the law.
A bigtime reason too is the strategic direction of a law firm. Why is someone desirous of working at your law firm? Is it the usual career grind and nothing more? Also, for the partners, are they willing to continue the usual course of a labor-based service delivery operation? The use of AI proffers not just potential changes in your existing labor-based service delivery, but also opens more strategic possibilities, such as productizing your legal services.
(48) Legal Aid Services and the democratization of law via AI
One bright hope about the use of AI in the law is that perhaps those that today are unable to afford legal services will be able to access legal services at a much lower cost. Imagine how this could demonstrably enable legal aid services.
Some even believe that AI in the law will democratize the law. They note that the law is often inaccessible, incomprehensible, or generally unavailable to a large portion of the population. If AI could perform legal tasks sufficiently, this would massively expand access to the law and make legal representation readily possible. The changes to society all told would be profound.
For more on this, see my analysis at the link here.
(49) Feared deskilling of lawyers due to the adoption of AI-powered lawyering
You might chuckle at this one, but perhaps give it a worthy shot anyway.
If AI can be sufficiently applied to the law, even if only as an aid to lawyers, will lawyers become reliant upon the AI and ergo tend toward a decay of their lawyering skills? Might the use of AI end up lulling lawyers into not remaining fully steeped in the law? Could we have a deskilling of lawyers?
I’m sure that you might be dubious or highly skeptical of this contention. The AI would have to be relatively capable and the lawyers would have to be using the AI quite a lot. It is an intriguing proposition. Food for thought.
For my coverage on this, see the link here.
(50) Potpourri of additional twists and turns about AI applied to the law
I’ve covered the tip of the iceberg about applying AI to the law. The same can be said about my discussion herein on the law as applied to AI. Lots more to be had. As you hopefully noticed, there are lots of fascinating and vital twists and turns associated with the AI and the law realm.

title: As Social Security official warns of A.I. fraud risks, one expert says criminal activity is 'here right now'
text:
While scrolling social media, you may find a video of President Joe Biden urging you to sign up for extra Social Security benefits for which you are eligible.
While the hypothetical video may seem real, the promise of extra benefits is not.
It's one example of the ways in which artificial intelligence may prey upon Social Security beneficiaries, according to Kathy Stokes, director of fraud prevention at AARP's Fraud Watch Network.
More from Personal Finance:
A.I. is on a collision course with white-collar, high-paid jobs
Big Four firm is trying to get teens interested in accounting
Disclosing a disability in the workplace
An unexpected communication can put anyone in a heightened state of emotion — and make them more susceptible to falling for such a scheme, she said.
If you divulge your personal information, you may be putting it in the hands of criminals who may redirect your monthly Social Security benefits to another account that is not yours.
"We're in this world where everything looks legitimate, but we can't trust anything," Stokes said.
A.I. fraud 'easier and faster to execute'
Artificial intelligence is generated by machines or software. Examples include ChatGPT, a chatbot enabled to have human-like conversations; deep fakes, phony audio or video made in someone's likeness; and generative A.I., which can create text or other media responses.
A.I. "will impact society in ways the public and private sectors are just beginning to understand," Gail Ennis, inspector general at the Social Security Administration Office of the Inspector General, wrote in a July letter to the agency.
Yet it's "imperative" to recognize the technology's potential risks, according to Ennis.
"The OIG understands criminals will use A.I. to make fraudulent schemes easier and faster to execute, the deceptions more credible and realistic, and the fraud more profitable," Ennis wrote.
The OIG has established an internal task force to study A.I. The goal is to determine the resources needed to prevent A.I.-related fraud, as well as to find out how to best use A.I. in the agency's oversight efforts.
The new initiative is already behind the curve, according to Haywood Talcove, CEO of the government business of LexisNexis Risk Solutions.
"You don't have years, months or weeks to study this, because it is here right now," Talcove said. "The criminals post pandemic are focused on government payments."
There are several reasons for that, Talcove said. For example, it's easy, there's "virtually zero" probability of getting caught and the government never runs out of money.
What's more, criminals are following government agencies as closely as beneficiaries, he said, by checking their web pages, reading blogs and generally trying to find as many vulnerabilities as possible.
You don't have years, months or weeks to study this, because it is here right now.Haywood TalcoveCEO of the government business of LexisNexis Risk Solutions
Social Security has long been susceptible to identity fraud and theft of benefits, noted Maria Freese, senior legislative representative at the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare.
A.I. fraud is the modern version of people having their checks stolen from their mailboxes every month, she said.
For the Social Security Administration, working to combat the new threats will pose a unique challenge after the agency has been underfunded for decades, Freese said.
"It's going to have to be expensive and it's going to have to be an ongoing effort," Freese said. "They need money to be able to deal with it."
3 features may be found in some 85% of scams
Consumers should be on high alert for signs of fraud, AARP's Stokes said.
That includes particularly watching for communication that comes out of the blue, puts you in a heightened emotional state and involves urgency, she said.
"Those three things together are what is the sign of probably 85% of scams," Stokes said.
It's also important to recognize that anyone — young or old — may easily fall for these sophisticated schemes, she said.
"When we're in that heightened emotional space in our brains, it's really hard to access logical thinking," Stokes said.
Other steps can also help protect your personal financial information and Social Security beneficiaries' monthly income, according to Talcove.
First, be sure to trace your credit at all three credit bureaus. Better yet, lock your credit so it is not accessible, Talcove said.
"One of the assumptions you can always make is your information has already been stolen," Talcove said.
Next, Social Security beneficiaries should notify the agency to contact them if the information tied to the bank account where their benefits are deposited changes, he said.
Additionally, everyone should change their their online Social Security password every month.
"I can't imagine what it would be like to be elderly and have to try to get through that system if my benefits were stolen," Talcove said.
"It's going to be the silent giant unless we address it," he said of potential criminal activity that can take place.

title: Big Tech's New Weapon Against Physician Burnout: Generative AI
text:
By 2034, the United States is projected to experience a shortage of up to 124,000 physicians as the demand for physicians outstrips supply. Physician burnout contributes significantly to this challenge, causing many to leave the workforce. One of the most frequently identified reasons for this burnout in the medical field is the growing burden of clerical tasks related to Electronic Health Records (EHRs) that clinicians must handle.
Major tech corporations are turning to Generative AI as a primary approach to tackle clinician burnout. However, despite their strong optimism and faith in Generative AI’s potential, healthcare CIOs are not plunging in as rapidly as expected.
Clinical Buy-In Falls Short
Clinicians have not yet adopted Generative AI for clinical decisions. Most use cases and press releases reflect the big tech's efforts to automate administrative tasks.
The American Medical Association (AMA) plans to formulate principles and recommendations addressing the benefits and pitfalls of generative artificial intelligence in healthcare. Besides creating recommendations, the AMA intends to collaborate with the federal government and other relevant organizations to shield patients from false or misleading AI-generated medical advice. Furthermore, the AMA has initiated and will continue to motivate physicians to educate their patients about AI engagement’s potential benefits and risks.
Jesse Ehrenfeld, President of the American Medical Association was not as hyped on Generative AI for clinical decision-making. He said “The algorithms are great for solving a textbook patient or a very narrow clinical question, but patients, they're not a standardized question stem. They're humans with thoughts, with emotions, with complex medical, social, psychiatric backgrounds. And I'll tell you, they rarely follow the textbooks.”
Dr. Ehrenfeld believes that Generative AI will reduce administrative tasks and considers it a valuable asset.
Privacy And Security Risk
Users of Generative AI must address privacy issues, security, intellectual property protection, and the evolving legal rules surrounding AI development and use. Currently, we have several lawsuits from comedians, authors, and more to come against OpenAI, Meta, and other tech companies on copyright infringement. We may have a similar scenario with healthcare data access.
Jake Dorst, Chief Information and Innovation Officer at Tahoe Forest Hospital District is also bullish on Generative AI and said “Generative AI has the potential to revolutionize the healthcare space in several ways. It can aid in medical image analysis, drug discovery, personalized treatment plans, and generating synthetic data for research”. He said, “Data privacy and security concerns are significant, as sensitive patient information needs protection.”
Big tech companies are in the initial phases of voluntary AI commitments, yet healthcare decision-makers must witness substantial progress before fully committing.
What Is Next?
While healthcare CIOs maintain a cautiously optimistic stance on Generative AI, it's worth highlighting the latest announcements from big tech regarding their newest AI innovations. These significant advancements illustrate the rapid pace at which this technology is progressing, despite the challenges and complexities that it presents.
Amazon
Amazon announced AWS HealthScribe, a new HIPAA-eligible service that allows healthcare software providers to develop clinical applications. Using speech recognition and generative AI, these applications produce clinical documentation, thereby conserving clinicians’ time.
Healthscribe is built on Amazon Bedrock and currently supports general medicine and orthopedics. Medical coding and transcription companies 3M and ScribeEMR, are early adopters of HealthScribe and will partner with AWS to use this service.
Microsoft
Microsoft took an early lead in conversational AI for generating clinical documentation by acquiring Nuance. In April 2022, Microsoft and EHR vendor Epic declared their partnership to incorporate Azure OpenAI Services. Recently, Teledoc, a virtual health provider, announced its intention to partner with Microsoft to integrate OpenAI services, automating the creation of clinical documentation during virtual exams.
Google is actively developing its large language model (LLM), Med-PaLM 2, which they anticipate will excel at healthcare discussions over general-purpose algorithms, given its training on questions and answers from medical licensing exams. They are collaborating with Mayo Clinic and other health systems and partnering with the healthcare technology vendor, CareCloud.
Every press release currently focuses on conversational Generative AI as a heralded solution to tackle burnout and automate administrative tasks. However, the question still lingers: is this reality or simply hype?
Punit Soni, CEO & Founder of Suki said "Generative AI is currently going through a hype cycle and getting a lot of attention. In six months' time, it's likely that the hype will settle. While gen AI will still have value, it will become clear that for these solutions to truly deliver meaningful impact, they will need to invest in strong foundational elements like EHR interoperability, secure and private infrastructure, an intuitive and flexible user experience that allows users to easily complete their tasks in whatever way works best for them, and an innovative mindset that builds quickly and at the cutting edge of what the tech can do. Without these, the impact of these solutions will be limited to niche use cases."
While AI may take some time to replace medical professionals, the current focus on alleviating administrative burdens is certainly a step in the right direction.

title: Council Post: Unleashing The Power Of AI: A Paradigm Shift In The Jewelry Industry
text:
Founder of New-York-City-based J'EVAR, ALTR Created Diamonds, Entrepreneur and third-generation Diamantaire.
The jewelry industry is experiencing a profound metamorphosis as it embraces the boundless possibilities offered by artificial intelligence (AI) technology. This reshaping of the industry is having an impact on sustainability, jewelry design innovation, renewable energy focus and the overall customer experience. Based on my experiences with using AI tools in my own company, let's explore some of the ways in which harnessing the power of AI algorithms is allowing these advancements.
AI's Role In Jewelry Design
The integration of AI-driven parametric tools is allowing jewelry designers to explore new possibilities, create innovative designs and push the boundaries of creativity. One of the key advantages of Design AI in the jewelry design process is its ability to analyze vast amounts of data and predict emerging trends with remarkable accuracy. By understanding shopper preferences, purchasing patterns and future customer trends, AI algorithms enable designers to tailor their jewelry design concepts to specific target audiences. This level of customization can help ensure that jewelry designs resonate with customers, enhancing their overall experience of creation and ownership.
AI-driven parametric tools also empower designers to explore intricate and complex designs that were once deemed impractical or time-consuming. For example, with 3-D printing, jewelry designers can now more easily create design concepts with intricate patterns, elaborate motifs and innovative structures. This newfound efficiency can allow designers to bring their vision to life faster than ever, resulting in a more diverse and captivating range of jewelry design concepts.
Enhancing The Consumer Experience
The integration of AI technology in the jewelry industry is also affecting the consumer experience. According to a study conducted by Salesforce, personalized experiences are considered a critical factor in the purchasing decisions of 84% of shoppers.
By utilizing a fusion of Design AI and Computer-Aided Design (CAD) software, the jewelry industry is equipped to meet these consumer expectations, delivering personalized and tailored experiences that leave a lasting impression. Whether it's through the creation of unique design elements or the ability to generate fresh ideas for custom pieces based on individual preferences, brands can use AI technology to empower their customers to actively participate in the design development process and co-create their own one-of-a-kind pieces. And leveraging AI predictive capabilities can allow the earth-mined and lab-grown diamond jewelry industries to anticipate evolving fashion trends so that their offerings align with ever-changing purchasing preferences.
AI-driven virtual try-on and augmented reality (AR) technologies have also emerged as powerful tools for enhancing the consumer shopping experience. Through virtual try-on platforms, customers can visualize how different jewelry pieces will look on them without physically trying them on. This immersive and interactive experience enables customers to make confident purchasing decisions while fostering a deeper connection with the jewelry brand. Respectable brands such as Tiffany, Cartier and Maria Tash are using this technology to improve their conversion rates as well as consumer confidence in their e-commerce platforms. Some are even working closely with institutions like MIT to further raise their level of consumer interactions.
Embracing A Sustainable Future
A recent study highlights the potential of AI technologies to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by up to 10%. This significant reduction can be attributed to the optimization and efficiency gains achieved through AI-driven processes across various industries, including jewelry. By leveraging AI algorithms, the industry has the potential to create a more sustainable and environmentally conscious approach to jewelry production and design.
From a supply chain perspective, AI algorithms offer significant opportunities to optimize resource utilization and reduce waste throughout the jewelry production process. By analyzing data and patterns, AI can identify areas of inefficiency and suggest improvements that minimize environmental impact. This includes optimizing inventory management, reducing energy consumption and streamlining logistics to minimize carbon emissions.
AI-powered tools could also enable designers to explore and experiment with sustainable materials and innovative manufacturing techniques. Take the example of 3-D printing again: Guided by AI algorithms, this technology allows for the creation of jewelry pieces using recycled metals. For example, the company Imaginarium offers over 140 materials for 3-D printing. This process could not only reduce waste but also reduce the industry's reliance on newly mined resources, contributing to a more circular and sustainable economy. By embracing AI and sustainable materials, the industry can reduce its carbon footprint and make significant strides toward a more sustainable future.
Challenges And Learning Curves
While AI has just begun to enter the fine jewelry industry, implementing this technology does come with a few limitations and learning curves. An initial barrier is simply obtaining high-quality and comprehensive data. If your brand is looking to enter this space, consider investing in data collection and collaborating with industry partners to help improve the accuracy of your AI algorithms.
It is also crucial to strike a balance between human creativity and AI assistance. Jewelry design is a highly artistic human process that simply cannot be completely tossed aside in favor of this new technology. Instead, focus on training programs and workshops to provide your designers with the skills to effectively incorporate AI tools. Learning to utilize these powerful tools takes time, so allow your employees to learn and grow their skills rather than try and make a hard shift. Those companies that follow best practices such as collaboration, training and ethical considerations in the jewelry business should be well-positioned to overcome the challenges associated with AI implementation and leverage its great potential.
Conclusion
I believe the future of the jewelry industry is intertwined with the limitless potential of AI-powered tools. Through this dynamic integration, sustainable elegance, innovation and ethical practices can converge, propelling the jewelry industry toward a more conscious and responsible future. As we witness the transformative power of AI in the jewelry sector, it seems clear that we are entering an era where technology, creativity and sustainability can harmoniously coexist, ultimately redefining the way we adorn ourselves with exquisite works of art.

title: Council Post: Generative AI Will Reshape The Future Of Business: How Employees Can Benefit From It And Shape Its Evolution
text:
Andrew Duncan, CEO and Managing Partner, Infosys Consulting.
As new technologies reshape the world of work, artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are accelerating the digital transformation. These innovations are profoundly impacting how business leaders think about and invest in their organizations in 2023. It has become clearer than ever that the businesses that are primed to thrive and capture new horizons of market share in the years ahead will be those that are underpinned by innovative new digital technologies.
The data backs this up. The global AI market is projected to reach $1,345.2 billion by 2030 according to MarketsandMarkets, with a CAGR of 36.8% from 2023 to 2030. In 2017, Gartner predicted that by the end of 2020, AI would create more than 2.3 million jobs.
Finally, research from the Infosys Knowledge Institute found that “firms that use AI well can increase enterprise profit by 38% and will help deliver $14 trillion of gross added value to corporations by 2035.” These are compelling statistics that clearly show our future trajectory.
I will share a few areas where I see generative AI as a key enabler to empowering employees, and thus powering new business opportunities ahead for organizations.
Generative AI Applied To Work
Generative AI has the transformative ability to reshape business processes, boost productivity and streamline repetitive tasks—all areas I see that can enrich the employee experience and complement how we as workers get our jobs done to maximum effectiveness.
Imagine a work world where we can spend less time on lower-value tasks (e.g., administration, research, report creation, customer support, etc.) and are able to engage our minds more in strategic thinking, decision-making, creativity and collaboration, for example. This is an AI-powered future that can benefit and enrich both the enterprise and individual alike.
1. Personalization In E-Commerce: Companies continue to seek out new ways to leverage their data and engage with consumers in a more effective way that can drive sales and increase profits. AI chatbots will continue to reshape this space and help companies to elevate and optimize their e-commerce platforms.
This type of generative AI can provide customers with deeper and more personalized information about products, pricing, search history and special offers, with no need to maintain an extensive customer support department.
Chatbots here can provide better and real-time responses to questions and searches, and act as a more advanced virtual shopping assistant of sorts. This is an area that can help back-end staff service more customers, focus on higher-value tasks or engage in other areas of a firm’s e-commerce operations.
2. Tracking, Managing And Optimizing In Logistics: Tremendous opportunities exist to drive operational efficiencies at scale and streamline efforts from back-of-house staff working in the logistics space. New advances and use cases in AI can offer better and more accurate information to help enhance communications, automate routine tasks and provide detailed insights into logistical operations.
All of this can improve performance, increase customer satisfaction and reduce costs for firms in this space. More specifically, route planning, package consolidation, route scheduling and fleet management can optimize capacity. I also see these areas enriching the employee experience with more access to data and empowering staff with better customer servicing insights.
3. Optimization Of Power Usage For Utilities: There’s no better time than today to conserve power and hopefully save costs for businesses and consumers alike. Utility providers have a treasure trove of data that can unlock profound new insights through the power of generative AI, which can help businesses improve their existing energy distribution strategy and ensure efficient use of resources.
I see the entire predictive maintenance space as a big beneficiary as well, as it can aid with advanced or real-time detection of operational issues, thus helping to reduce downtime and maintenance costs. Workers stand to benefit here, as their roles can shift upward in the value chain.
4. Supporting Sales Efforts: Massive opportunity exists to support and aid sales professionals with their planning and customer engagement, potentially making them more effective and increasing top-line performance for their companies. Through generative AI, better recommendations can be produced from CRM tools based on customer sentiments via engagement activity in emails, websites and social media activities.
In fact, Salesforce recently rolled out Einstein GPT, an advanced AI tool to gain better customer insights and tailor more personalized messages to targets—which promises a quantum leap in productivity.
Things To Keep In Mind
However, not all the implications of generative AI are positive. It is essential for businesses to be aware of the limitations and mitigate the risks of emerging AI technology before embarking on this path to digital transformation.
For example, without clear and ethical guidelines for AI technology used in an enterprise setting, the potential business value could be undermined by misinformation or bias built into the AI algorithm. This is especially important for organizations in regulated industries, such as healthcare, pharmaceutical manufacturing, banking and insurance.
It’s clear that generative AI will dramatically influence the organization of today and of the future. The question I leave you with is this: How do we govern and utilize AI in the most responsible way that can enrich our daily work experiences while adding bottom-line value to the enterprise? I look forward to your thoughts and feedback.
